title: The Tenth Guru's writings close

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading one line of his, carried through a whole day. Your line was one line, one day. Which line did you choose, and where did it show up? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

Lay four things on a table. A hymn that won't stop praising. A life story told in verse. A letter that tells an emperor he broke his word. A love song sung in the wilderness. Four things that hardly seem to belong to one person. They do. For a long run of days we've been reading Guru Gobind Singh's writings, and today the block closes. Before we move on, let's pick up each of the four, and then find the one thread that runs through all of them.
screen: `FOUR THINGS ON A TABLE.` → `ONE PERSON WROTE THEM ALL.` → `ONE THREAD THROUGH THEM.`

segments.voice: Praise first. The Jaap Sahib and the Akal Ustat pour out names for the Timeless One: without mark or sign, without caste or lineage, without color or form. And inside that praise, the line that recognizes the human race as one. Then autobiography. The Bachitar Natak tells his own story: his father who gave his head but not his faith, the battle at Bhangani, and his warning that no one should call him God, because he is only the servant. Then rebuke. The Zafarnama tells an emperor plainly that oaths were broken, and still holds that no one can harm the one the Lord protects. And song. The ten shabads include the one Sikhs call the song from the wilderness. In paraphrase: tell the beloved Friend how it is with his disciples; without You, fine comforts feel like sickness; a straw bed with the Friend is better than a palace without. Now the thread. Every one of the four starts from the same place: praise of God, said out loud, without hedging. The letter of rebuke opens with praise. The life story is written in the servant's voice, which is a kind of praise. The love song longs for the Friend. Even in loss, even writing to the man whose armies chased him, the Tenth Guru praises first and boldly. That's one thread a reader can take from this shelf of writings. Not a mood of gloom, and not a mood of triumph, but praise that doesn't wait for a good day.
screen: `PRAISE: NO MARK, NO CASTE, NO FORM.` · `AUTOBIOGRAPHY: ONLY THE SERVANT.` · `REBUKE: YET STILL PROTECTED.` · `SONG: A STRAW BED WITH THE FRIEND.` · then, large: `BOLD PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise once, boldly. Settle, and breathe. Then, if you pray, say the name Waheguru out loud once, not whispered, in a full voice, and let the sound fill the room. If you don't pray, say out loud one thing you're grateful for, as plainly and fully as you can. Don't wait for a good day to do it. Then sit in the quiet that follows until the bell, and notice how the room feels after a word said boldly. The bell holds the time.
The Tenth Guru's writings close. Praise, autobiography, rebuke and song, all held together by praise said out loud, even in loss. Today's word.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU'S WRITINGS CLOSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bold praise. Today, say one good thing about someone out loud, to their face or to others, without softening it. Tomorrow a new block begins: the Khalsa and its code. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tenth Guru's Jaap Sahib and swayyas in the morning prayers, sing his shabads in kirtan, and hear the Zafarnama and Bachitar Natak in katha, the teaching sessions of the gurdwara.

fork.setup: you've lost almost everything and you're writing to the man responsible. how does the Tenth Guru begin?
fork.reveal: the Zafarnama opens with praise. across all four kinds of writing, praise comes first and boldly.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pile of different old writings.
what it means: praise, autobiography, rebuke and song, from one person.
what a scholar hears: one thread under all four: praise said out loud first, even in loss, even to an emperor.
